subtype: Family adjusting to a shift worker [Receiver]
passage: Kashish beti, you think you're the first wife to eat dinner alone? Sit with your Yamini Dadi a minute. When I was twenty-four, your Dada worked nights at the steel plant. For months I kept his plate covered and ate with only the radio for company. On Diwali he slept through the lamps, and I sulked for two days. He came home grey with tiredness and said sorry so often it stopped meaning anything. Then one morning, instead of sulking, I sat him down with his tea. On the back of the calendar we wrote a promise: Sunday lunch together, no matter what. I hung a thick curtain and told the children, 'Papa's sleeping, play in the courtyard.' And he told me honestly when he was too tired to talk. That is how we stayed friends.

qa.q: What promise did Yamini and Dada write on the back of the calendar?
qa.a: Sunday lunch together, no matter what.

qa.q: How did young Yamini feel when Dada slept through Diwali?
qa.a: She felt neglected and hurt, and she sulked for two days.

qa.q: What was the turning point in those night-shift years?
qa.a: The morning Yamini sat Dada down over tea instead of sulking, and they planned shared time, a quiet house for his sleep and honest talk.

qa.q: How did Dada seem to feel about missing family life?
qa.a: He seemed guilty and worn out, coming home grey with tiredness and apologising so often that the word lost its meaning.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a wife who feels neglected as a shift worker misses meals and festivals, his guilt and tiredness, and how planned shared time, quiet for sleep and open talk held them together.

subtype: Family adjusting to a shift worker [Receiver]
passage: Keerthana worked from home, taking customer calls in the only room of the flat she shared with her sister Trisha. Trisha, a nurse, had been on nights for weeks, sleeping through the day behind a bedsheet hung from the ceiling. Keerthana whispered into her headset for hours and felt like a ghost in her own home. Then Trisha slept through Keerthana's birthday dinner. 'You're never here, even when you're here,' Keerthana said that night. Trisha's eyes filled. 'I know. I hate it too.' They couldn't afford a bigger place. So they made a plan: Keerthana would take morning calls from the building's quiet reading room, Trisha would set an alarm for Sundays, and every Sunday they'd eat breakfast together before Trisha slept. The first Sunday they made dosas and talked until the sun was high.

qa.q: Where did Trisha sleep in the flat?
qa.a: Behind a bedsheet hung from the ceiling.

qa.q: How was Keerthana feeling when she said, 'You're never here, even when you're here'?
qa.a: She felt lonely and neglected, like a ghost whispering all day in her own home.

qa.q: What made their plan work despite the small flat and little money?
qa.a: They talked openly first, then shared the load: morning calls from the reading room, a Sunday alarm and a fixed breakfast together.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel about missing the birthday dinner?
qa.a: Trisha felt guilty and sad; her eyes filled and she admitted she hated it too.

grounding: Shows a sister feeling neglected by a shift worker who feels guilty, and how shared time, quiet for sleep and open talk hold them together despite a small flat.

subtype: Business traveller and a tired mind [Observer]
passage: Mehak noticed it the moment Manoj walked into the spice-packing unit at Kumily. He had flown back from a trade fair in Germany the night before and caught the early bus up the ghat. At the morning meeting he snapped at the foreman over a small spelling slip on a label, then dozed off with his chin on his hand while the cardamom prices were being read out. When a trader from Bodi arrived wanting a quick yes on a large order, Mehak stepped in. 'Sir only got back yesterday. Can we give you an answer on Wednesday?' The trader shrugged and agreed. At lunch Mehak slid a glass of lime juice across the table. 'Go home early, sir. The order will keep.' Manoj rubbed his eyes and, for once, did not argue.

qa.q: What did Manoj do while the cardamom prices were being read out?
qa.a: He dozed off with his chin on his hand.

qa.q: What was Mehak thinking when the trader wanted a quick yes?
qa.a: Mehak was worried that Manoj, worn out from the long trip, might misjudge a large order, so stepped in to buy time.

qa.q: Why was asking for an answer on Wednesday a fair and practical choice?
qa.a: It gave Manoj a few days to recover from the trip before a big decision, without refusing the trader.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt when Mehak told him to go home early?
qa.a: He probably felt tired and a little relieved, too worn out to argue, and perhaps grateful that someone had noticed.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing someone back from a long trip being irritable and dozing in a meeting, and fairly delaying a crucial decision to give time to adjust.

subtype: Adapting wisely to a disrupted clock [Response]
passage:
Supervisor's note, cabin crew base. Written by Sachin.
Arohi joined our long-haul roster in January. I have watched how she handles the time changes and want to record it for new crew. She keeps the same sleep window at every hotel, whatever the local time, with blackout curtains and an eye mask, and she steps outside into morning light when she needs to wake up. She carries fruit and eats proper meals instead of living on snacks from the trolley. Last month she asked me to hold her answer on a transfer until she had slept, and she was right to. When tiredness and low mood did not lift, she booked a visit to the company doctor. What I did next: I asked Arohi to speak to the new crew on Friday.

qa.q: What does Arohi use at the hotel to protect her sleep window?
qa.a: Blackout curtains and an eye mask.

qa.q: Why did Arohi ask Sachin to hold her answer on the transfer?
qa.a: She was wary of trusting her own judgment while short of sleep and wanted to decide with a rested mind.

qa.q: What could new crew learn from Arohi's approach?
qa.a: Guard a fixed sleep window, use light and darkness on purpose, eat proper meals, delay big decisions until rested, and see a doctor when low mood does not lift.

qa.q: How does Sachin see Arohi's habits?
qa.a: Sachin respects them enough to record them as an example and asks Arohi to speak to the new crew.

grounding: Shows a person on a disrupted clock guarding a fixed sleep window, using light and darkness, eating sensibly, delaying a decision while tired and seeing a doctor when low mood persists.

subtype: Adapting wisely to a disrupted clock [Response]
passage:
Tuesday, 11:40 p.m.
Third week on the overseas support shift. Old Samir would have powered through on chai and fried snacks and then wondered why everything felt grey. New rules, and I kept every one today:
Slept nine to four with foil on the window and my phone in the other room. Ujjwal knows not to knock.
Went for a walk in the evening light before logging in, to tell my brain it's 'morning'.
Ate proper dal-rice at seven instead of chips.
My manager wanted an answer on the team-lead offer tonight. I said I'll reply on Friday, after my off days. Tired Samir says yes to everything.
If this heaviness doesn't lift, I'm booking the doctor. Promised Amma on the phone.

qa.q: What did Samir eat at seven?
qa.a: Proper dal-rice instead of chips.

qa.q: What is Samir worried about when it comes to the team-lead offer?
qa.a: Samir is worried that a tired mind says yes to everything, so wants to decide after rest.

qa.q: Which of Samir's new rules seems most important, and why?
qa.a: Guarding the sleep window in a dark, quiet room, because steady sleep supports mood and judgment; the walk in the light also helps the body clock.

qa.q: What is it like for Ujjwal to share a home with Samir on these hours?
qa.a: Ujjwal has to stay quiet in the day and not knock, which takes patience but lets Samir sleep.

grounding: Shows a person on a night-time schedule guarding a fixed sleep window, using light and darkness on purpose, eating sensibly, delaying a big decision and planning to see a doctor if low mood persists.

subtype: Toddler recharging after a big day [Actor]
passage:
'Ayesha, come! Show Nani your zoo pictures!' Nani called from the doorway.
Ayesha, two, lay on the floor clutching her cloth elephant.
'Ayesha? Come and say hello.'
'No!' She kicked her feet and began to wail.
Her mother Seema knelt beside her. 'Big day, na? So many animals.'
Ayesha crawled into Seema's lap and pressed her face into her kurta.
'Amma, let's do the pictures tomorrow,' Seema said.
Nani smiled and dimmed the lamp.

qa.a: Her cloth elephant.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt when Ayesha shouted 'No!'?
qa.a: Nani may have been a little disappointed but understood, and dimmed the lamp to help Ayesha rest.

grounding: Shows a toddler worn out after an outing who wants quiet, a familiar toy and closeness, and falls apart when pushed to do more.

subtype: Toddler recharging after a big day [Actor]
passage:
Note for Zeenat's parents, from Jeevan at playgroup.
Today we visited the fire station. Zeenat loved the red truck and waved at every siren. Back at playgroup she refused circle songs, threw a block and cried when asked to join. I stopped asking. She carried her blue blanket to the reading corner and leaned against me while I read softly. She napped for a long time. Please expect a quiet evening; rest helps her take in a big day.

qa.q: Where did Zeenat carry her blue blanket?
qa.a: To the reading corner.

qa.q: Why might Zeenat have thrown a block after the trip?
qa.a: She was likely tired and overwhelmed after the exciting visit, so being pushed to join songs felt like too much.

qa.q: What did Jeevan try once Zeenat started crying, and why did it help?
qa.a: Jeevan stopped asking her to join and let her rest with her blanket and a quiet story, which gave her the calm she needed.

qa.q: What would change if Zeenat's parents planned a busy evening?

subtype: Quiet time as a skill [Response]
passage: Every afternoon after lunch, the flat in Pune went quiet for a while. Five-year-old Eshaan used to hate it. 'Boring!' he'd moan, rolling on the rug. His father Tenzin didn't argue. He simply lay on the sofa with his own book while soft flute music played. One day Eshaan dragged his crayons over and drew a whole train, carriage by carriage. When the music ended he looked up, surprised. 'Papa, can quiet time be longer tomorrow?'

qa.q: What did Eshaan draw during quiet time?
qa.a: A whole train, carriage by carriage.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel about quiet time at first?
qa.a: He felt bored and fed up, moaning 'Boring!' and rolling on the rug.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin's approach work better than arguing?
qa.a: By resting with his own book and music, Tenzin showed quiet time was worth having, so Eshaan found his own calm activity.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see quiet time?
qa.a: Tenzin seems to see it as real rest, not laziness, which is why he joins in himself.

grounding: Shows a young child who learns to spend a short, calm time drawing to gentle music and finds it restful, with a parent who shows quiet time is not laziness.

subtype: Quiet time as a skill [Response]
passage:
'Jomon Sir, why is the light off here?'
'It's the resting corner, Devika. Just a short time. You can pick a book or listen to the rain music.'

The little bell tinkled.
'Already? Can I finish the whale?'
'Of course you can.'

subtype: Child needing downtime after school [Actor]
passage: The school bus dropped Trisha at the edge of the village at four, dusty and silent. Her father Anand looked up from mending the fence. 'How was the test? Did Ma'am return your notebook? Who won at kho-kho?' Trisha dropped her bag. 'Nothing.' Then, sharply, 'Leave me!' Anand opened his mouth to scold, then remembered his own long schooldays. He handed her a guava from the tree and said only, 'The goats need taking to the pond.' Trisha walked them down alone and threw pebbles into the water for a long time. At dinner she told him everything, even the kho-kho score.

qa.q: What did Anand hand Trisha?
qa.a: A guava from the tree.

qa.q: What does Trisha's sharp 'Leave me!' suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was drained and irritable after a long school day and needed space before any questions.

qa.q: What made Anand's second response better than his first?
qa.a: Instead of more questions or a scolding, he offered a snack and time alone with the goats, so she could recover and chose to talk later.

qa.q: What was it like for Anand when Trisha snapped at him?
qa.a: He was tempted to scold but remembered his own schooldays, and was rewarded when she told him everything at dinner.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild silent and irritable after a long day who needs a snack and time alone before talking, and later opens up.

subtype: Child needing downtime after school [Actor]
passage: Jana's key turned in the door of the apartment in Oslo at half past three. She kicked off her boots, walked past her father Lars without a word, and shut herself in her room. Lars had a list of questions ready: the spelling test, the class trip form, her friend's birthday. He looked at the closed door and put the list away. Instead he cut an apple, spread a little peanut butter on the slices, and left the plate outside her door with a knock. For half an hour there was only the sound of building blocks clicking together. Then Jana came out, plate empty, and leaned on the kitchen counter. 'Pappa, guess what happened at recess.'

qa.q: What did Lars leave outside Jana's door?
qa.a: A plate of apple slices with a little peanut butter.

qa.q: What might Jana have been feeling when she walked past Lars without a word?
qa.a: She was probably tired and overloaded after a long school day and wanted to be alone before talking.

qa.q: What could other parents learn from Lars's choice?
qa.a: Holding back the questions and offering a snack and quiet play time lets a child recover, and often they start talking on their own.

qa.q: If you were Lars looking at the closed door, what would you be tempted to do?
qa.a: You might want to knock and ask all the questions at once, or feel shut out, but waiting gave Jana room and brought her back chatting.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild silent after a long day who needs time alone and a snack before talking, and a parent who finds that works better than immediate questions.

subtype: Teen packed with classes and coaching [Actor]
passage: I'm Francis, Sarita's classmate, and we've shared a bench since Class 6. This year her week is school till two, maths tuition till five, physics coaching till eight, and dance on Saturdays. She eats lunch while copying notes. Last month she stopped laughing at anything. When I asked about the weekend she said, flatly, 'What weekend?' Once she pushed her textbook away and muttered that she hated all of it. Then her mother suggested she drop dance for a term, and Sarita kept Saturday afternoons empty: she lay on the terrace, read comics, walked to the lake with her cousin. Now she answers in physics quicker than before. I can't be sure what changed inside, but her laugh is back.

qa.q: Until what time is Sarita's physics coaching?
qa.a: Till eight.

qa.q: How was Sarita feeling when she said, 'What weekend?'
qa.a: She felt flat and resentful, worn out by a week with no room to rest.

qa.q: What change helped Sarita, and why?
qa.a: Keeping Saturday afternoons free for the terrace, comics and walks gave her mind room to recover, and she seemed sharper in class.

qa.q: How does Francis see the change in Sarita?
qa.a: Francis can't know what changed inside her, but notices that her laugh is back and that she answers quicker in physics.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a teenager packed with school, tuition and activities who feels flat and resentful until free time is built into the week.

subtype: Teen packed with classes and coaching [Actor]
passage: Monday, June: Indu's alarm rang at five. School, then chemistry tuition, then entrance coaching, then an online mock test late at night. By Thursday she was crying over a spilled bottle of ink, heart racing, sure she was falling behind everyone. Sunday, a week later: her sister Payal sat down with her and the timetable. 'Where's the part where you just exist?' Indu couldn't find one. Together they crossed out the late mock test and wrote FREE across Wednesday evening. Wednesday, three weeks on: Indu sat on the balcony with Payal, shelling peas and humming, doing nothing important. In Thursday's test she remembered a formula she had been fighting with for days. 'Huh,' she told Payal. 'It stuck.'

qa.q: What did Indu and Payal write across Wednesday evening?
qa.a: FREE.

qa.q: What was Indu worried about when she cried over the spilled ink?
qa.a: She felt anxious and was sure she was falling behind everyone, with no time left to rest.

qa.q: Which step was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Crossing out the late mock test and keeping Wednesday evening free, because the rest gave her mind room to recover and even helped a formula stick.

qa.q: How does Payal seem to see Indu's timetable?
qa.a: Payal sees that it has no space for Indu simply to be, and treats free time as necessary rather than wasted.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a packed schedule of school, tuition and coaching who feels anxious and flat, and recovers once free time is built into the week.

subtype: Guilt about resting [Actor]
passage: Sunday afternoon in Jaya's rented room in Hyderabad, and nothing was due. She lay on the bed for ten minutes, then sat up, heart thumping. Lazy. She opened her laptop, closed it, reorganised her pens, and felt worse. Her friend Darshan, dropping off a borrowed book, found her pacing. 'You look like you're waiting for an exam result,' he said. 'I'm just wasting the day.' Darshan shrugged. 'Remember last month? You studied every single Sunday and fell asleep in the practical.' Jaya remembered. They walked to the lake, ate roasted corn and said nothing much. On Monday she finished her lab report in half the usual time and noticed, with surprise, that she didn't mind.

qa.q: What did Jaya and Darshan eat by the lake?
qa.a: Roasted corn.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when she lay on the bed with nothing due?
qa.a: She felt guilty and anxious, calling herself lazy, so the rest felt empty rather than restful.

qa.q: What helped Jaya see rest differently?
qa.a: Darshan reminded her that overwork had left her asleep in the practical, and after a real break she finished her report faster, showing rest improves later work.

qa.q: How did Darshan see Jaya's pacing?
qa.a: He saw that she was stressed, not resting, and gently reminded her of last month.

grounding: Shows a young adult who feels lazy and anxious whenever not being productive, and learns that genuine rest makes later work better.

subtype: Guilt about resting [Actor]
passage:
The office had emptied when Arohi, his teammate, stopped at Jatin's desk.
'Jatin, it's nine. Why are you still here?'
'Just finishing the slides.'
'You finished them at six. I saw.'
'Then I'll check the numbers again.' Jatin rubbed his eyes. 'If I go home I'll just sit there feeling useless.'
'Useless how?'
'Last Sunday I watched a film and spent the whole time thinking I should be working. Couldn't enjoy a minute.'
'You know your best pitch was the week after Holi, when you'd taken four days off?'
'That was luck.'
'Was it? You were sharp. You laughed in meetings.'
Jatin went quiet. 'So rest is... part of the work?'
'It's what makes the work good. Go home. Take a walk. Leave the laptop shut.'
He saved the file and, slowly, closed it.

qa.q: When did Jatin actually finish the slides?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel while watching a film last Sunday?
qa.a: He felt guilty and anxious, thinking he should be working, so he couldn't enjoy the rest.

qa.q: What turned Jatin's thinking around?
qa.a: Arohi reminded him that his best pitch came after four days off, helping him see rest as part of doing good work.

qa.q: How does Arohi see Jatin staying late?
qa.a: Arohi sees it as unnecessary and worrying, since the slides were done, and cares enough to send Jatin home.

grounding: Shows a young adult who feels useless and guilty whenever not working, and a teammate who helps him see that recovery makes later work better.

subtype: Rest that actually restores [Response]
passage: Friday, early March: Keerthana spent her free evening in bed with her phone, thumb moving for hours. She went to sleep somehow more tired, jaw tight. Saturday, a week later: her friend Yamini dragged her to a pottery class above the bakery. Keerthana's hands were caked in clay, the wheel wobbled, and she forgot to check anything for two whole hours. Walking home, she noticed her shoulders had dropped. That night she made a list: pottery, walks by the sea, dinners with Yamini, plain quiet with the window open. Late April: Keerthana's work calendar had a block every Saturday afternoon marked 'maintenance'. When her manager asked for a weekend call, she offered Monday instead.

qa.q: Where was the pottery class?
qa.a: Above the bakery.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel after the evening on her phone?
qa.a: She felt more tired and tense, jaw tight, as if the scrolling had not rested her at all.

qa.q: What might Yamini have noticed about Keerthana after the pottery class?
qa.a: Yamini may have seen a looser, lighter friend with dropped shoulders, compared with the tense one Yamini had dragged along.

subtype: Rest that actually restores [Response]
passage: Sumit, you asked how I lasted thirty years on the wards. I'll tell you. At twenty-four I was a young nurse in Goa: work, then collapse in front of the television, then work again. I thought rest was a treat you had to earn. I snapped at patients' families. One evening my friend Lourdes, from the same ward, said, 'Maria, when did you last swim?' I had loved the sea as a girl. That Sunday I swam at dawn and came back hungry and laughing. So I made a rule: Tuesday and Sunday mornings, the sea, whatever happened. Some weeks the matron grumbled. I went anyway, the way you oil a machine. I was a kinder nurse for it. Now tell me, Sumit, what is your sea?

qa.q: What did young Maria do at twenty-four?
qa.a: Maria worked as a young nurse in Goa.

qa.q: How did young Maria feel after swimming at dawn that Sunday?
qa.a: Maria felt refreshed and happy, coming back hungry and laughing.

qa.q: What choice turned things around for young Maria?
qa.a: Making a rule to swim on Tuesday and Sunday mornings whatever happened, treating it as upkeep rather than a treat to be earned.

qa.q: How might Lourdes have seen Maria before that Sunday swim?
qa.a: Lourdes probably saw a worn-out friend who snapped at families and had lost touch with what Maria loved, which is why Lourdes asked about swimming.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a person discovering that the sea, not television, truly refreshed Maria, and protecting that time each week as maintenance rather than a reward.

subtype: Colleague or partner respecting a need for rest [Observer]
passage: Nadia heard Dalia's key in the door at nine, two hours late again. Their flat in Lisbon smelled of the soup Nadia had made. Dalia dropped her bag and stood in the hallway, still in her coat, staring at the shoe rack. Nadia had planned to ask about the weekend trip to her own parents' village. She looked at Dalia's grey face and put the question away. 'Soup's warm. Bath's running. You don't have to talk.' Dalia's eyes filled. 'Sorry. I'm useless tonight.' 'You're tired. That's different.' Nadia texted her mother that they might come a week later. Later Dalia fell asleep on the sofa with her head on Nadia's knee. On Saturday morning she woke first and made coffee for them both, humming.

qa.q: What had Nadia made for dinner?
qa.a: Soup.

qa.q: What was Nadia thinking when she saw Dalia's grey face?
qa.a: Nadia felt concerned and decided the weekend question could wait, seeing that Dalia was worn out.

qa.q: Which of Nadia's choices helped most?
qa.a: Offering soup, a bath and no need to talk, and quietly moving the visit, gave Dalia space to recover without guilt.

qa.q: What was it like for Dalia to be met with soup and no questions?
qa.a: Dalia felt guilty and close to tears at first, calling herself useless, but being allowed to rest let her recover and wake up humming.

grounding: Shows a woman who sees the person she shares a home with depleted, holds back her own plans and offers space and practical relief, which helps them recover without guilt.

subtype: Colleague or partner respecting a need for rest [Observer]
passage: In the staffroom of the girls' school, Karthik watched Vinita mark the same answer sheet for the third time. She had covered two absent teachers' classes all week and stayed late for the science fair. Now the principal's message pinged: someone was needed to run Saturday's parents' meeting. Vinita reached for her phone to volunteer. Karthik got there first. 'I'll take Saturday,' he typed. Then, to her: 'And give me half those sheets. You're done for today.' Vinita opened her mouth to protest, then laughed weakly and handed them over. 'I owe you.' 'You don't. Go home and sleep.' The next Monday she came in with her usual jokes and a box of homemade laddoos, which she left on his desk without a word.

qa.q: What had Vinita covered all week?
qa.a: Two absent teachers' classes.

qa.q: What was Karthik thinking when Vinita reached for her phone to volunteer?
qa.a: He was worried that she was already exhausted and would overload herself, so he stepped in first.

qa.q: How did Karthik offer practical relief?
qa.a: He took the Saturday meeting and half the marking and told her to go home, without making her feel guilty about it.

qa.q: How did the break seem to affect Vinita?
qa.a: She came back on Monday with her usual jokes and left laddoos for Karthik, which suggests she felt rested and grateful.

grounding: Shows a coworker seeing a colleague depleted and taking tasks off her instead of pushing, and how being allowed to recover strengthens their working bond.
